interactions.summary: Jiang says Chinese primary schooling rapidly kills curiosity, empathy, and vitality, turning eager first-graders into obedient blank-eyed children within a year or two.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang answer continuing the prior question

interactions.summary: The host asks whether official reform efforts exist inside the Chinese education system.
Jiang says reform is universally acknowledged as urgent, but grassroots parents resist it because Gaokao still looks like the only mobility ladder for families without exit options.
The host asks where teachers stand in the conflict over reform.
Jiang says teachers want the best for students but remain bound to the test system emotionally and professionally, which leaves reform trapped in a communication and trust gap.

claims.claim: Jiang says Chinese schools kill a child's curiosity, creativity, imagination, and empathy within one or two years of entry.
claims.temporal_scope: Current diagnosis on 2014-06-19 based on Jiang's school visits.

claims.claim: He says teachers discipline questioning itself, teaching students that asking questions marks them as troublemakers.
Jiang says education reform is now seen across China as urgent and as something that will determine the country's future.
He says a 2010 education reform blueprint called for more individuality, creativity, freedom, less homework, and more time for children to play and explore their interests.
claims.temporal_scope: Retrospective description on 2014-06-19 of a 2010 reform blueprint.

claims.claim: Jiang argues poorer or less mobile families resist reform because Gaokao still appears to be their only credible route to upward mobility and reform looks like elite sabotage of that route.

He says teachers genuinely want the best for students but still double down on test training because success in the system is measured by exam performance and they fear students will fall behind otherwise.
Jiang says the reform impasse is partly a communication failure between top-level reformers and grassroots families and educators.

signature_moments.moment: The classroom ideal becomes a child standing obediently in line with blank eyes.
signature_moments.source_phrase: their eyes are kind of blank, kind of lifeless
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang's critique of schooling a memorable human image instead of an abstract policy complaint.

signature_moments.moment: A child asking questions is recoded from engaged learner into classroom troublemaker.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if you ask questions, you're a troublemaker
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's compact mechanism for how curiosity gets destroyed inside everyday teaching practice.

signature_moments.moment: Reform is not opposed because people love the old system; it is opposed because they think elites are sabotaging the poor family's only ladder upward.
signature_moments.source_phrase: sabotaging their only way to increase their social mobility
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Jiang's political reading of why obvious educational reform still stalls.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's name for the publicly launched reform agenda that called for more individuality, creativity, freedom, and less homework in Chinese schools.
The less affluent parents, teachers, and local actors who experience reform as risk rather than liberation.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang situates the reform fight in 2014 as downstream of a publicly announced 2010 education reform blueprint.

uncertainty_notes.note: The transcript identifies the official only as 'Prime Minister Wang...' with an incomplete name, so the summary keeps the reform blueprint claim without over-specifying the officeholder.
